implementation_notes: The gateway is an interface plus an injected client: a gateway method awaits client.GetResponse<OrderStatusResult>(request, cancellationToken) and MassTransit publishes the request with a response address, correlates the reply and completes the returned Task; a consumer exception comes back as Fault<T>, which the client rethrows as RequestFaultException. What replaces the classic gateway class is the request client plus the message contracts - you write the domain interface and the request/response records instead of the send-correlate-parse loop. The hand-written route (RabbitMQ.Client with ReplyTo/CorrelationId, as in the .NET RPC tutorial) is only justified when the stack cannot take a bus dependency.
pitfalls: Cancelling GetResponse only stops waiting: the request message stays on the queue until it is consumed or its time-to-live expires (the TTL defaults to the request timeout, 30 seconds), so a timed-out call can still execute remotely.
A failing consumer is reported as Fault<T> and rethrown as RequestFaultException, so the original stack trace does not survive the boundary.
Request messages are published by default and must be consumed by exactly one endpoint; adding a second consumer silently turns the request into load-balanced work.
Resolving IRequestClient per call instead of injecting the singleton costs an extra bus endpoint and wastes the first-request latency.

variants.name: Hand-written async facade over RabbitMQ.Client
variants.idiom_name: gateway class with CallAsync over BasicPublishAsync/BasicConsumeAsync (ReplyTo + CorrelationId)
variants.implementation_notes: Without a bus, the gateway is the class from the .NET RPC tutorial: an exclusive callback queue declared at construction, CallAsync generating a correlation id, publishing with ReplyTo/CorrelationId and awaiting the matching delivery. What the classic class needs here is precisely what a framework would have generated: the correlation table, the reply dispatch and the timeout. Choose this route when adding a broker library is acceptable but a bus framework is not - for example inside a small service or a library that must not dictate the messaging platform.
pitfalls: The reply consumer runs on its own thread, so the waiting caller needs an explicit handoff (a TaskCompletionSource); blocking the dispatch thread deadlocks the client.
One callback queue per client plus a correlation table is the documented design - declaring an exclusive reply queue per call multiplies broker objects for every request.
Nothing times out by itself: with no server running the call waits indefinitely unless WaitAsync/ct carries a deadline (the tutorial lists exactly these unsolved gaps).
Unknown correlation ids must be discarded, not thrown on: a restarted consumer can answer the same request twice.
